subsections.title: U.S.-China / Trump-Xi
subsections.text: Presidents Trump and Xi are meeting on the sidelines of the APEC Summit in Shenzhen (18–19 November), their third encounter this year. China has confirmed a historic first trilateral with Russian President Putin on 19 November focused on “safeguarding world peace,” strategic stability, and nuclear non-proliferation. Trump has indicated topics will include denuclearisation, the Iran conflict, trade, and Ukraine. Post-midterm U.S. results have led some Chinese analysts to reassess Trump’s capacity to deliver on bilateral commitments, even as the personal relationship remains transactional. The existing framework emphasizes a “constructive and strategically stable relationship based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity.” Super-intelligence (SI) dialogue channels on model evaluation, human control, and incident reporting continue. Taiwan arms sales remain held in abeyance. Expectations for major deliverables are modest, with further trade-truce extensions or agricultural/rare-earth progress the most plausible outcomes.

subsections.title: U.S.-Iran / Middle East / Houthis
subsections.text: Tensions remain elevated. The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group has entered the CENTCOM area, bringing the U.S. presence to three carriers. Iran conducted drone strikes targeting a U.S. radar site in Bahrain (intercepted, no reported damage). In Yemen, Houthi forces have advanced near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, forcing internationally recognized government-aligned forces to withdraw from coastal positions to defend Aden. Iran continues to refuse IAEA access to damaged nuclear sites until the conflict is “permanently ended.” Trump has signaled possible restraint on further strikes absent fresh provocations, while Gulf partners (Saudi, Bahrain, UAE) remain under pressure from drone/missile activity.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: Fighting continues at high intensity (day ~1,727). Russia claims to have intercepted over 1,300 Ukrainian drones in a major overnight attack, including hundreds toward the Moscow region; Ukraine struck the Crimean (Kerch) Bridge, temporarily limiting traffic. Russian strikes continue to target Ukrainian energy and rail infrastructure. Zelenskyy has highlighted restrictions on Starshield satellite use as a constraint on defenses. U.S. proposals involving territorial concessions (e.g., Donbas) in exchange for security guarantees have been floated; Trump has described Putin as “backing down a little.” Peace process remains stalled ahead of Ramstein and Coalition of the Willing meetings.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: China has formally extended the Busan-era trade truce until 10 January 2027. It has suspended the additional 24% tariff on U.S. goods (retaining a 10% blanket rate), paused certain rare-earth and critical-mineral export controls, and suspended special port fees on U.S.-linked vessels. The United States has correspondingly extended Section 301 tariff exclusions on 178 Chinese product categories and suspended related port fees. Key monitoring points remain Chinese agricultural purchases (soybeans, coal) and rare-earth flows. The Boards of Trade and Investment established earlier in 2026 provide structured channels; a ~$30 billion package of reciprocal non-sensitive tariff reductions remains under discussion. The Shenzhen meetings offer a near-term window to lock in further extensions or incremental progress before the January cliff.

sections.title: Energy Markets & Oil Prices

subsections.text: WTI settled near $85.72 and Brent near $92.44 on 16 November (declines of ~3.2% and ~3.6% respectively), with further softness into 17 November. Key drivers include recovering Persian Gulf/Hormuz export flows and the IEA’s assessment of a return to surplus in Q4 2026 (~1.7 mbd). Vice President Vance has publicly signaled that the United States does not intend a prolonged commitment in the Iran theater. Risks remain elevated: continued shipping incidents, Houthi consolidation near Bab el-Mandeb (affecting Red Sea routes), and the potential for renewed escalation. Short-term outlook is biased lower on surplus signals and recovering volumes, though a geopolitical risk premium persists and any major disruption could reverse the decline quickly. Goldman Sachs sees Brent averaging ~$88 in 2027 before further softening as surplus conditions normalize.

sections.title: Inflation, Monetary Policy & Bond Markets

subsections.text: October U.S. CPI rose 0.4% m/m (headline) and 0.3% m/m (core), with year-over-year estimates around 3.9% headline and ~2.8–2.9% core. Labor-market data remain solid (initial claims near 200k). The federal funds target range stands at 3.75–4.00%. Markets now price a very high probability (~90–100%) of a 25 bp hike at the 9 December FOMC meeting, with some officials (including Governor Waller) having floated the possibility of 50 bp if inflation remains firm. The 10-year Treasury yield is trading in the 5.12–5.15% area. The European Central Bank is also expected to tighten further. Energy-related and AI-driven price pressures continue to complicate the path back to 2% targets. Higher-for-longer policy rates and elevated term premia remain the dominant features of the bond market.

sections.title: AI Capex Boom & Supply-Chain Risks

subsections.text: Hyperscaler capital-expenditure guidance for 2026 is concentrated at roughly $700–725 billion (Amazon ~$200 bn, Alphabet ~$175–185 bn, Microsoft and Meta in the $115–190 bn range). This wave is crowding out conventional electronics production and stretching lead times for PCBs, laminates, and specialty materials. Persistent bottlenecks include high-bandwidth memory (HBM), advanced packaging (CoWoS capacity still constrained despite expansion plans), optical components, power transformers, grid connections, and critical minerals. China continues to dominate refining of rare earths, gallium, and germanium (>90% in several categories); the current export-control suspensions run only until mid-January 2027. Power availability and transmission infrastructure are emerging as binding constraints on data-center deployment timelines. Concentration risk across a small number of suppliers (foundry, memory, lithography, packaging) remains structurally high.

subsections.title: U.S.-China relations / Trump-Xi follow-ups
subsections.text: Preparations are advancing for the third Trump-Xi summit of 2026 on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen (18–19 November), with a further encounter expected at the G20 in Florida in December. Agenda items include trade commitments under the Boards of Trade and Investment, agricultural and rare-earth purchases, and super-intelligence (SI) risk management (pre-release model evaluation, human control, and an incident-reporting channel). Secretary of State Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi have coordinated logistics; Treasury Secretary Bessent is accompanying Trump. A possible U.S.-China-Russia trilateral on the APEC sidelines has been confirmed by the White House, focusing on Iran and nuclear issues rather than Ukraine. Post-midterm Republican losses have slightly improved Beijing’s near-term negotiating leverage, though longer-term congressional pressure on Taiwan arms sales and export controls remains. A low-level military crisis-management framework is under discussion, though analysts note it is inadequate for nuclear or major flashpoint crises.

subsections.title: U.S.-Iran conflict & Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: Iran and its allies intensified pressure over the weekend. The IRGC claimed drone attacks on U.S. radar sites at Riffa Air Base in Bahrain (disputed by CENTCOM, which reported intercepts with no damage). Iranian naval forces alleged mines struck tankers near the Strait of Hormuz. In Yemen, Saudi-backed government-aligned forces withdrew from Red Sea coastal positions near Bab al-Mandeb and Dhubab, allowing Houthi advances that threaten the approaches to Aden; Houthis also launched ballistic missiles toward Saudi targets. President Trump has indicated to advisers he may hold off on further strikes absent fresh provocations, favoring economic pressure. Shipping through Hormuz remains disrupted relative to pre-conflict norms.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: Day ~1726–1727 of the full-scale invasion saw continued high-intensity fighting (171 combat engagements reported on 14 November) and reciprocal long-range strikes on energy, industrial, and civilian infrastructure. Russian personnel losses were estimated by Ukrainian sources at ~2,230 in the prior 24 hours (cumulative ~1.62 million). U.S.-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi produced no breakthrough; U.S. negotiators reportedly floated Ukrainian NATO membership in exchange for full withdrawal from Donbas—an idea rejected by Moscow’s maximalist demands. Ukraine continues deep strikes on Russian oil facilities. Front lines have seen limited net Russian gains in recent months amid high attrition. Other developments include Estonia’s decision to close border crossings with Russia following a reported sabotage attempt and ongoing Black Sea shipping risks.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: China formally extended the suspension of its additional 24% tariff on U.S. goods for two months (through 10 January 2027), retaining a 10% blanket tariff. Parallel extensions cover special port fees on U.S.-linked vessels, certain export-control and entity-list measures, and rare-earth-related waivers. The United States likewise extended relevant Section 301 exclusions and related pauses. These steps implement the September Washington summit consensus that prolonged the Busan-era truce. Reciprocal tariff reductions on roughly $30 billion of non-sensitive goods per side remain under discussion via the Board of Trade, alongside agricultural purchase commitments. No major new tariff actions were announced in recent days; both sides continue to press for fuller implementation of existing pledges ahead of the Shenzhen summit. China has flagged that it will monitor any U.S. shift toward Section 301 tariffs as a replacement for previously invalidated IEEPA measures.

subsections.text: Trilateral talks (Ukraine, Russia, U.S.) took place in Abu Dhabi this week, with discussion of expanding future rounds to include European representatives and working toward a large-scale prisoner exchange (potentially up to 1,500 per side). Positions remain firm: Russia insists on Ukrainian neutrality, demilitarization, and territorial elements; Ukraine and the West emphasize security guarantees. Starshield satellite system speed restrictions have limited Ukrainian interception capabilities. A Russian warship was reportedly struck in the Gulf of Finland. Overall trajectory points toward a possible negotiated endgame, though core gaps on territory and security architecture persist. Day count is approximately 1,725.

Differences persist on Taiwan (including a held-up U.S. arms package), advanced chip export controls, rare-earth supply reliability, and agricultural purchase fulfillment. Beijing is prioritizing stability into its 2027 Party Congress preparations, while Washington post-midterms faces domestic pressure on technology controls and enforcement of prior commitments. Ukraine conducted one of its largest drone attacks of the war (nearly 1,200 drones targeting Russian regions, including oil infrastructure and the Moscow area), while Russian forces struck Ukrainian cities including Odesa, Zaporizhzhia, and Kyiv-area targets. U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have facilitated talks that produced progress on a major prisoner exchange and Russian agreement to include European representatives in future rounds; however, no breakthrough has occurred on territorial demands, security guarantees, or foreign troop presence. Putin has maintained a hard line against foreign peacekeepers and continues to press maximalist positions. In the Middle East, the U.S.-Iran confrontation remains in a coercive economic and limited-military phase rather than full-scale combat. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has stated there is currently “no need” for major combat operations because economic pressure (including an expanded naval and land blockade via Task Force Iron Gate) is effective. Regional spillover risks to shipping and Saudi facilities remain elevated.

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: The Japanese yen has again tested the psychologically important 160 level against the dollar (trading near 159.7–160 as of November 13–14), marking the third such test in 2026. Japanese authorities have spent roughly ¥27 trillion year-to-date supporting the currency, including record single-day operations. Prior joint U.S.-Japan intervention (July–August) involved only modest U.S. participation (~$0.5 billion), which has reduced the perceived deterrent of coordinated action. Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama, top currency official Atsushi Mimura, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi have issued warnings against “one-sided” and rapid moves and reaffirmed readiness to act. The wide U.S.-Japan interest-rate differential continues to underpin yen weakness; the Bank of Japan has held at 1.25% but is widely expected to consider a hike in December as underlying inflation has reached its target. Broader central-bank trends show a tilt toward further tightening in response to sticky inflation driven in part by energy prices and prior tariff effects.

subsections.text: The relationship remains framed around “constructive strategic stability” based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity. Presidents Trump and Xi held summits in Beijing (May) and Washington (September). A third is scheduled for the APEC summit in Shenzhen on 18–19 November, with a fourth planned for Miami in December. subsections.title: U.S.-Iran conflict & Middle East (including Houthis)
subsections.text: The conflict is ongoing (day ~257 as of 11 November). The U.S. continues an economic pressure/blockade campaign while major combat operations remain limited. Attacks on Gulf shipping continue. On the Houthi front, mutual strikes persist: Houthis have targeted Saudi infrastructure (including claims against Riyadh-area targets, Aramco facilities, and airports), while Saudi-led forces have conducted interceptions and strikes inside Yemen. Fighting also continues in Yemeni government-aligned areas.

subsections.title: Ukraine-Russia
subsections.text: Intense frontline fighting continues (125 clashes reported in one recent day; heaviest in Kostiantynivka and Pokrovsk sectors), with heavy Russian drone/missile use and Ukrainian long-range strikes on Russian energy, ports, and military production. Ukrainian drone activity has disrupted a significant share of Russian refining capacity. US-brokered trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi have produced progress on a large-scale prisoner exchange and some mutual understanding, with Ukrainian officials expressing hope for results by year-end. Territorial issues, security guarantees, European role, and trust remain major gaps. Kremlin framing emphasizes broader European security architecture. No major frontline territorial shifts were recorded in the most recent ISW assessment. Other developments remain secondary to the above flashpoints.

sections.title: Trade Wars & Tariffs

subsections.text: China has formally extended the Busan-era trade truce measures by two months to 10 January 2027. The additional 24% Chinese tariff on U.S. goods stays suspended; a 10% blanket tariff remains. Port fees on U.S.-linked vessels, certain export-control and entity-list measures, and related restrictions are also paused through the same date. On the U.S. side, the reduced fentanyl-related tariff (10% rather than 20%), suspension of Section 301 maritime measures, and extended Section 301 exclusions continue. Reciprocal recommendations for more favorable treatment on ~$30 billion of non-sensitive goods each way (agricultural, energy, consumer, and other items) were advanced via the Board of Trade, though final implementation details and timing remain subject to domestic procedures. Soybeans were notably excluded from some lists. The Shenzhen APEC meeting is the near-term focal point for possible further extension or additional deals. Both sides continue to press the other on full implementation of prior commitments (agriculture, rare earths).

sections.title: Macro Currency Interventions

subsections.text: The yen remains under pressure. USD/JPY has traded near 159 recently (around 158.7–159.8 in latest closes), approaching levels that previously triggered intervention risk. Japan conducted large yen-buying operations in late July–early August (including a record single-day purchase of ~¥7.98 trillion and a multi-day total of ~¥15.4 trillion), with the first coordinated U.S.-Japan intervention since 1998 on 31 July. The Finance Ministry has confirmed the actions and maintains a readiness to act against disorderly moves. The BoJ has raised rates (most recently to 1.25% in September, with board splits), and further tightening is expected, but the wide policy-rate gap versus the Fed continues to favor the dollar. Verbal and rate-checking signals have been used; fresh intervention risk rises if the pair approaches or clears 160. Broader central-bank trends show the Fed and ECB leaning tighter on inflation risks while the BoJ continues its gradual normalization from ultra-low rates.
